answers.answer: Yes, at the family level. In SCOPe 2.08 (the current release per /api/v1/, with latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16), d1s9za_ (sunid 98768, chain 1s9z A) and d1hqja_ (sunid 61142, chain 1hqj A) both carry SCCS k.40.1.1 and sit under the same family node, sunid 100905, 'Designed trimeric coiled-coil'. Their protein-level nodes are 'Amyloidogenic design-1' (sunid 103785, the parent of d1s9za_) and 'Unnamed design-1' (sunid 100906, the parent of d1hqja_), which are sibling proteins under that family. Under SCOPe's definition, family membership is a classification of common evolutionary origin, so SCOPe does treat these two as homologous. Limits: (1) These are designed proteins, not natural sequences with a phylogenetic ancestor. The shared family reflects SCOPe's classification of a shared designed coiled-coil architecture, so the 'homology' is a curatorial statement about the design template and should not be read as descent from a natural ancestor or as sequence identity. (2) Do not transfer the 'Amyloidogenic' label from d1s9za_ to d1hqja_, and do not infer amyloid-forming or any other function from family co-membership. The protein-level names are design labels, not functional annotations. (3) Family membership does not establish sequence identity or a specific functional relationship. Confirming the relationship independently would need a sequence or structure comparison of the two chains, which I did not run here. (4) This applies to SCOPe 2.08 only. Family assignments may differ in other releases.

answers.answer: Yes, at the family level. In SCOPe 2.08 (the current release per /api/v1/, with latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16), d1s9za_ (sunid 98768, chain 1s9z A) and d1hqja_ (sunid 61142, chain 1hqj A) both carry SCCS k.40.1.1 and sit under the same family node, sunid 100905, 'Designed trimeric coiled-coil'. Their protein-level nodes are 'Amyloidogenic design-1' (sunid 103785, the parent of d1s9za_) and 'Unnamed design-1' (sunid 100906, the parent of d1hqja_), which are sibling proteins under that family. Under SCOPe's definition, family membership is a classification of common evolutionary origin, so SCOPe does treat these two as homologous. Limits: (1) These are designed proteins, not natural sequences with a phylogenetic ancestor. The shared family reflects SCOPe's classification of a shared designed coiled-coil architecture, so the 'homology' is a curatorial statement about the design template and should not be read as descent from a natural ancestor or as sequence identity. (2) Do not transfer the 'Amyloidogenic' label from d1s9za_ to d1hqja_, and do not infer amyloid-forming or any other function from family co-membership. The protein-level names are design labels, not functional annotations. (3) Family membership does not establish sequence identity or a specific functional relationship. Confirming the relationship independently would need a sequence or structure comparison of the two chains, which I did not run here. (4) This applies to SCOPe 2.08 only. Family assignments may differ in other releases.
